nameStory: The "globefruit" part of this plant's name comes from its distinctive round, globe-shaped seed capsules that look like tiny green marbles. The "primrose-willow" name reflects its membership in the evening primrose family, even though it doesn't look much like either primroses or willows! This confusing name is why botanists sometimes prefer the more descriptive "globe-fruited false-loosestrife."
description: Globefruit primrose-willow is a low-growing wetland plant that hugs the muddy edges of ponds, streams, and marshes. It spreads along the ground with creeping stems that can extend several feet, forming loose mats in shallow water or wet soil. The small, oval leaves grow directly opposite each other along reddish stems, and tiny yellow flowers appear in summer where the leaves meet the stem. Its most distinctive feature is the perfectly round seed capsules that give it its common name.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: The round, globe-shaped seed capsules are unmistakable - they look like tiny green marbles about the size of a peppercorn sitting at the base of each leaf pair. These smooth, hard capsules are what make this species unique among New England's wetland plants.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, smooth oval leaves grow in pairs directly opposite each other along the stem. The leaves feel somewhat thick and waxy to the touch, and are typically bright green with a slight sheen that helps them shed water.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny yellow flowers with four petals appear tucked into the leaf joints (called axils) rather than at the stem tips. The flowers are so small - barely larger than a pinky nail - that you might miss them unless you look closely.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms spreading mats by sending out creeping stems that root at the joints where leaves emerge. The plant stays low to the ground, rarely rising more than a few inches above the water or mud surface.

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, often reddish or purplish stems that feel firm and slightly succulent. The stems have a distinctive four-angled or square cross-section that you can feel by rolling them gently between your fingers.

habitat: Look for this rare plant in the muddy shallows of clean ponds, slow streams, and freshwater marshes, often growing right at the water's edge where it can be partially submerged. It prefers sandy or silty soils and clean water with little pollution. In New England, it's most often found in coastal plain ponds and river backwaters, typically growing alongside other wetland plants like water purslane and various sedges.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges from overwintered roots in late spring, with fresh green leaves appearing as water levels drop. The spreading stems begin to extend and root at this time.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with tiny yellow flowers blooming from June through August. The distinctive round seed capsules begin forming shortly after flowering and are most noticeable in late summer.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and turn brown, eventually splitting to release seeds. The above-ground portions begin to die back as temperatures drop, though some stems may persist into early winter.
seasonality.winter: The plant dies back to underground roots and is not visible above ground. Look for last year's dried stems and seed capsules frozen in ice or washed up on shore as clues to where it might return.

funFact: This plant is so rare in New England that it's been spotted only 6 times by nature observers in the entire region, making it one of the botanical world's best-kept secrets - you're more likely to see a bald eagle than find this tiny wetland gem!
confusionNotes: Most likely to be confused with its cousin water purslane, but water purslane has tiny green flowers and egg-shaped (not perfectly round) seed capsules. Remember: "Globe-shaped capsules = globefruit primrose-willow, egg-shaped = water purslane."
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name, this plant isn't closely related to true primroses or willows at all - it's in the evening primrose family. The "false-loosestrife" name also adds confusion since it's not related to true loosestrifes either. Being listed as endangered in multiple New England states means disturbing or collecting this plant is illegal and could harm already struggling populations.
compareHints: Unlike its relative water purslane which has alternate leaves and tiny green flowers, globefruit primrose-willow has opposite leaves and yellow flowers. The seedbox, another cousin, is much taller and upright rather than creeping, and has larger, more obvious flowers. The perfectly round seed capsules are unique to globefruit primrose-willow among all the primrose-willows in our region.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Water purslane differs from its Ludwigia relatives like seedbox and globefruit primrose-willow by its tiny, inconspicuous flowers and low, mat-forming growth habit.

Seedbox stands out from its primrose-willow relatives by its cube-shaped fruits and alternate leaves - water purslane has opposite leaves and tiny flowers, while globefruit primrose-willow has round (not square) seed pods.
